Project grounding for this story-writer instance — mock3.

Scope. Two tickets, one per codeline:
- MOCK3-1 — Riders aged exactly 65 are charged the adult fare. Lives in codeline mocka at /home/bradleyjerome/projects/mock3/mock-a, in src/fares.ts, covered by test/fares.test.ts.
- MOCK3-2 — The departure board omits the final stop. Lives in codeline mockb at /home/bradleyjerome/projects/mock3/mock-b, in the formatStops rendering path in src/schedule.ts, covered by test/schedule.test.ts.

Both codelines declare the same stack: typescript with vitest. Write stories that assume TypeScript sources under src/ and colocated vitest specs under test/, and nothing else about the layout — the project context does not describe further structure, so do not invent directories, config files, or module boundaries that were not named above.

Roles a story may be assigned to. Three were minted for this project, and story scoping must match them:
- fare-schedule-engineer (implementer) — spans both codelines. Both tickets are single-line pure-function logic fixes in the same declared stack, so implementation stories for src/fares.ts and src/schedule.ts both land on this one role. Do not split implementation into per-codeline stories that imply two separate implementers.
- mocka-detective (investigator) — scoped entirely to mocka: confirm the exact comparison operator in src/fares.ts and the current boundary coverage in test/fares.test.ts.
- mockb-detective (investigator) — scoped entirely to mockb: confirm the actual loop bound in formatStops and the current coverage in test/schedule.test.ts.

Ordering that the roles imply. Each ticket's investigation story precedes its implementation story. The survey lead that produced these tickets is unverified; the detectives exist precisely so the implementer does not act on it alone. A story that asks the implementer to change a comparison or a loop bound before the corresponding detective has confirmed what is actually there is mis-ordered, however obvious the fix looks.

Traps specific to these two tickets. Both are boundary defects, and boundary defects are where an imprecise story does real damage:
- MOCK3-1 turns on inclusive-versus-exclusive comparison at the senior threshold (>= against >, or the age constant sitting on the wrong side). A story must state which side of 65 is meant to be the senior fare, because "fix the age check" admits both a correct and an off-by-one-wrong reading.
- MOCK3-2 turns on an exclusive loop bound dropping the last element. A story must state that the final stop is expected in the rendered output, not merely that the loop bound is wrong.
- For both, the acceptance criterion belongs at the boundary value itself — exactly 65, and the last stop in the list — not at a comfortably interior value that passes either way.

Since these are pure functions with existing vitest specs, a story's verification step is a vitest run over the affected codeline plus a TypeScript type-check. Do not write a specific command line, flag set, or script name into a story: the project context declares vitest and typescript as dependencies but does not record how this project invokes them, and a fabricated command is worse than an unspecified one because the agent will run it.

Name only what appears above — codelines mocka and mockb, files src/fares.ts, test/fares.test.ts, src/schedule.ts, test/schedule.test.ts, the symbol formatStops, and the tickets MOCK3-1 and MOCK3-2. Any other file, symbol, package, or command in a story is an invention.
